title: TentNetFA: A convolutional neural network
text:
What TentNetFA does
TentNetFA maps likely tent locations from high-resolution satellite imagery. It is designed for a difficult operational problem: settlements can grow, move, and change quickly, while a conventional field count may be unavailable, delayed, or unsafe to conduct. The output is a point map that can be aggregated into grids or administrative areas and used alongside other evidence in population nowcasting.
The method is not a way to identify people, households, or individual tents with certainty. It is a repeatable process for turning a satellite scene into an estimate of where tents are likely to be concentrated. Those estimates need to be interpreted with the imagery date, local conditions, and independent information in mind.
TentNetFA was developed from a tent-mapping effort with Forensic Architecture using Planet satellite imagery and annotated tent locations created by a dedicated group of volunteer students at the University of Oxford. Its outputs support our wider population-nowcasting collaboration with humanitarian partners as well as Forensic Architecture’s mission to compile evidence for justice and accountability. The active implementation is maintained in our TentNetFA source repository which is a fork of the original Algorithmic Governance repository.






Figure 1: Volunteers manually annotate satellite imagery during the training-data effort run by the Algorithmic Governance Foundation.



Image credit: Algorithmic Governance Foundation, “Tracking Conflict Displacement in Gaza with Machine Learning.”

title: TentNetFA: A convolutional neural network
text:
The method in one view
The current workflow has two connected pipelines:

Build training examples from dated imagery and tent annotations, then fit a convolutional neural network (CNN).
Apply the fitted model to new imagery, convert its continuous output into points, and merge duplicate detections from overlapping tiles.

The important idea is that the CNN does not directly answer a yes-or-no question for every pixel. It predicts a smooth tent-density surface. A separate, explicit post-processing step then turns peaks in that surface into tent points. Keeping these steps separate makes it possible to inspect and tune the rules that determine how many points are ultimately reported.

title: TentNetFA: A convolutional neural network
section: Training data: imagery, annotations, and change
text:
Training data: imagery, annotations, and change
Training begins with Planet GeoTIFF scenes and geographically referenced tent annotations. The annotations were originally produced for the Forensic Architecture mapping effort. For each training scene, TentNetFA selects annotations for the relevant date and rasterises the point locations into the coordinate system of the image.
Large scenes are divided into small, overlapping tiles. In the current configuration, each tile has a 70-metre core and a 15-metre margin on every side. The margins give the model context around the core and reduce edge artefacts. They also mean that the same ground location can occur in more than one prediction tile; the final merge step is therefore essential.






Figure 2: Examples of annotated image tiles used to construct training data. Magenta marks show tent annotations; red lines show the tile grid.



Each tile contains three related RGB images:

the current satellite image;
a pre-war reference image covering the same location; and
the channel-wise difference between the current and reference images.

Together these form a nine-channel input. The reference and difference layers help the model distinguish features that were already present from changes that may be associated with temporary shelter. They are useful evidence, not a guarantee: damage, rubble, agriculture, shadows, image quality, and other changes can also produce strong differences.
Before a tile is passed to the model, its image bands are standardised so that one scene’s overall brightness does not dominate another’s. The exact standardisation mode is recorded in the resolved configuration for a run. This does not make images identical, but it gives the model a more stable numerical scale on which to learn.

From points to a learning target
A tent annotation is a point, but a point is too sparse to be a useful target for a pixel-level model. TentNetFA therefore converts every annotated point into a small Gaussian-shaped bump and adds the bumps together. The result is a density map: locations close to an annotated tent receive high values, and nearby pixels receive lower values that fade with distance. This family of approaches—learning a continuous surface from point annotations—has a long history in object-counting research (Lempitsky and Zisserman 2010).
This representation gives the CNN a smoother learning problem. Rather than having to reproduce a single exact pixel, it learns to place a peak near each annotated tent. It also preserves a useful interpretation: summing the density surface over an area approximates the number of annotated tents in that area.
The width of the Gaussian is a modelling decision. A very narrow target approaches a hard point label and becomes sensitive to small alignment errors. A very broad target makes nearby tents harder to separate. TentNetFA records this setting with the training configuration so that the target surface can be reproduced.
Training data contain many tiles without tents. The pipeline retains only a configured fraction of these empty tiles when it builds the balanced training manifest. This prevents the model from learning the unhelpful rule that every location is empty simply because empty pixels are common.

title: TentNetFA: A convolutional neural network
text:
The convolutional neural network
The model is a compact CNN that accepts the nine-channel tile and returns one channel: a predicted density surface with the same spatial layout as the input. It combines several convolutional layers with batch normalisation and rectified linear activation functions. Dilated and wider convolutional layers give the model a larger local field of view without reducing the output resolution.
During training, the model compares its predicted density surface with the Gaussian-smoothed annotation surface using pixel-wise mean squared error. The checkpoint with the lowest validation loss is saved for prediction. The implementation uses PyTorch for the model, optimisation, and batched data loading (Paszke et al. 2019). This evaluation is useful for selecting a model during fitting, but it is not a complete measure of operational accuracy: a low density-map loss does not by itself show that point counts are reliable in every place, settlement type, or date.

title: TentNetFA: A convolutional neural network
section: From a density surface to tent points
text:
From a density surface to tent points
The model’s output is continuous. To produce a point map, TentNetFA applies a transparent sequence of selection rules.
First, it calculates a local-context score. The raw predicted density is combined with a Gaussian-blurred version of the same surface. The blur rewards a candidate that sits near other predicted tents and reduces the influence of isolated peaks, which are often more likely to be noise or visually similar features. The relative weight of this neighbourhood contribution is a configuration parameter.
In simplified notation, the selection score at location \(x\) is
\[
s(x) = p(x) + \alpha\, [G_\sigma * p](x),
\]
where \(p(x)\) is the model’s raw density prediction, \(G_\sigma * p\) is its Gaussian-smoothed neighbourhood signal, and \(\alpha\) controls how strongly nearby predictions contribute. The score is not a calibrated probability that a tent exists at \(x\); it is a ranking signal used to select candidates.






Figure 3: Schematic of point selection distinguishing a cluster of tents from isolated rubble, a potential source of false positives. The upper curve represents local prediction peaks; adding a broad Gaussian neighbourhood signal increases support for clustered peaks while leaving an isolated peak relatively less competitive at a fixed threshold.



Next, non-maximum suppression identifies local peaks in that score surface. A candidate must be the largest value within a small neighbourhood and must exceed the configured selection threshold. Tile margins are cropped from the candidate search so that edge predictions are not counted twice.
Finally, detections from all tiles are merged. Points closer together than the configured minimum distance are deduplicated, and optional inclusion or exclusion zones can be applied. The result is written as a geospatial point layer with the raw peak value and the adjusted, neighbourhood-aware score.
The merge stage uses a spatial index to find nearby candidates efficiently, then checks their geographic distance before combining them. This matters because prediction tiles overlap by design: without global deduplication, the same visual feature could become two output points.
Thresholds, neighbourhood weighting, and merge distance are not cosmetic settings. They change the balance between missed tents and spurious detections, and therefore change the resulting counts. They should be selected against independent evidence for the imagery, geography, and operational question at hand—not treated as universal model constants.

title: TentNetFA: A convolutional neural network
text:
Parameters that shape the output
TentNetFA keeps its settings in a resolved configuration file for each run. This is important for reproducibility, but the settings are also methodological choices: they determine what information reaches the model and how a predicted surface becomes a point map. The table below describes the settings that are most important for interpreting or adapting the method. It deliberately describes their role rather than prescribing values.







Parameter group
What it changes




Tile core and margin (core_metres, margin_metres)
The area predicted at a time, the amount of contextual imagery around it, and the extent of overlap between neighbouring tiles.


Valid-data threshold (min_valid_fraction)
Whether a tile with black, missing, or invalid imagery is retained for training or prediction.


Empty-tile retention (null_keep_fraction)
The balance between tent-free and tent-containing examples during training.


Standardisation (per_tile_standardisation)
Whether brightness is normalised separately for each prediction tile or at a wider image scale.


Point-selection method (selection.method)
Whether locations are taken from local score peaks (nms) or the centres of predicted blobs (centroid).


Selection threshold and neighbourhood factor (selection.threshold, selection.factor)
How strong a candidate must be, and how much support from nearby predicted signal contributes to its selection score.


Peak spacing (nms_kernel_size, selection.min_distance_m)
How close two selected peaks can be before they are treated as alternatives rather than separate candidates.


Global merge rules (merge.min_distance_m, merge.agreement, merge.min_adj_peak)
How predictions from overlapping tiles are combined and filtered into the final point layer.


Geographic zones
Whether points are retained only inside, or removed from, specified geographic areas.



These settings interact. For example, lowering a selection threshold may recover faint tents but can introduce visually similar false positives; increasing the merge distance can reduce duplicate detections but can also combine nearby real tents. A defensible configuration is therefore one evaluated against relevant independent evidence, not simply the configuration that produces the largest count.
The TentNetFA repository records the resolved configuration and runtime behaviour for each run. The settings described here should be reported alongside any published output so that its methodological choices can be inspected and reproduced.

title: TentNetFA: A convolutional neural network
text:
Validation and quality assessment
Validation has two jobs. The first is to assess the learned density maps during model development. The second is to assess the final point product after all selection and merging rules have been applied. Both matter because point extraction can improve or degrade a useful density prediction.
Threshold and neighbourhood-weight sensitivity analyses show why a single Strip-wide count is not enough: settings that improve agreement with an independent map in one area can introduce spurious detections in another. This is why point-selection settings need to be assessed at the same spatial scale and in the same kinds of landscapes as the intended use of the results.






Figure 4: An example sensitivity analysis for an earlier workflow. Each cell represents a combination of the point-selection cutoff and neighbourhood-weighting factor; the stars identify settings selected under different objectives. These values are historical illustrations, not the active pipeline’s universal parameters.



For the active pipeline, validation should use an independent source wherever possible and report results at the spatial scale at which the map will be used. Useful checks include visual review of sampled tiles, comparison of counts in a common grid, error by settlement density or land cover, and comparison across image dates. The repository includes tools for point-level and grid-based comparisons, but their results are specific to the validation data and settings used.

title: TentNetFA: A convolutional neural network
text:
Limitations and responsible use
TentNetFA is sensitive to the data and assumptions that enter it.

Annotations are a partial reference, not perfect ground truth. Missed, inconsistent, or temporally mismatched labels can be learned by the model.
Satellite scenes vary. Clouds, haze, shadows, resolution, season, viewing conditions, damage, and image-processing choices can alter what tents look like.
Change is not uniquely a tent. The pre-war comparison helps focus attention on new features, but construction, debris, agricultural structures, and other changes can resemble shelter.
Post-processing encodes decisions. A threshold or merge distance that is reasonable in a dense camp may not be reasonable in a sparse or damaged area.
A point count is not a population estimate. Tent locations must be combined with carefully stated assumptions and other data before they are used to infer the number of people in an area.

For these reasons, the maps should be used as one input to humanitarian analysis, alongside field knowledge, manual review, and other independent data sources. They are most useful when their uncertainty, date, coverage, and intended aggregation scale travel with the result.

title: TentNetFA: A convolutional neural network
text:
Software and data products
TentNetFA is a Python project managed with Poetry. Its main software roles are deliberately separated:

Raster and coordinate handling: Rasterio, Fiona, PyProj, GeoPandas, and Shapely read satellite rasters and vector data, transform coordinates, and write spatial outputs.
Array processing and point selection: NumPy and SciPy support standardisation, Gaussian filtering, connected components, and spatial search.
Model fitting and inference: PyTorch loads tiles in batches, trains the CNN, and evaluates new imagery.
Run orchestration: the repository’s pipeline runner resolves the configuration, records logs, and keeps the artifacts from every processing stage together.

The main intermediates are intentionally inspectable: tile manifests are stored as Parquet tables, per-tile predictions as GeoJSON, and the deduplicated final product as a GeoPackage. A checkpoint alone is therefore not sufficient to reproduce a map. Reproduction also needs the input imagery, reference raster, annotation snapshot where relevant, and the resolved configuration that records tile geometry, standardisation, selection, and merge settings.

title: TentNetFA: A convolutional neural network
text:
Reproducibility and adaptation
The repository separates configuration from code. A run records the resolved configuration, intermediate tile manifests, prediction files, model checkpoint, and final merged output. This makes it possible to reproduce a particular map and to compare alternative configurations without silently changing the processing chain.
Anyone adapting the method to another setting should treat the model, labels, imagery, reference imagery, and point-selection parameters as a single system. Reusing a checkpoint without local validation is unlikely to be reliable: tent materials, backgrounds, image providers, and the meaning of a temporary structure can all change from one context to another.






NoteFurther technical detail



The current pipeline, configuration reference, and evaluation utilities are available in the TentNetFA repository. This chapter describes the method and its decisions; it is not a step-by-step deployment guide.

title: Practical Tutorial: Posteriors, Likelihoods, and Priors
Practical Tutorial: Posteriors, Likelihoods, and Priors
text:
Analysis Script
Once you have model_of_the_mean.stan saved into your R working directory, run the following script to simulate new data and refit the model using MCMC.
First, let’s just setup our R environment and working directory.

# cleanup
rm(list = ls())
gc()
cat("\014")
try(dev.off(), silent = T)

# check working directory
getwd()

# [optional] update/fix working directory
# setwd(file.path('/my/working/directory/model_of_the_mean'))

# directories
wd <- getwd()

Then, we’ll simulate data and run the model.

# load libraries
library(cmdstanr)

#---- SIMULATE DATA ----#

# set seed for random number generators
seed <- round(runif(1, 1, 1e6))
set.seed(seed)

# simulated population parameters
mu <- 5 # true population mean
sigma <- 3 # true population standard deviation

# simulate observations
n <- 1e3 # sample size
y <- rnorm(n = n, mean = mu, sd = sigma)

# Stan model data
md <- list(
  n = n,
  y = y,
  mu_true = mu,
  sigma_true = sigma,
  seed = seed
)

# save data to disk
saveRDS(object = md, file = file.path(wd, "md.rds"))


#---- MCMC ----#

# compile the stan model
mod <- cmdstan_model(file.path(wd, "model_of_the_mean.stan"))

# function to generate initial values
init_generator <- function(md = md, chain_id = 1) {
  result <- list()

  result[["mu"]] <- runif(1, -1e3, 1e3)
  result[["sigma"]] <- runif(1, 0, 1e3)

  return(result)
}

# MCMC configuration
chains <- 4
warmup <- 1e3
samples <- 2e3
inits <- lapply(1:chains, function(id) init_generator(md = md, chain_id = id))

# run MCMC
fit <- mod$sample(
  data = md,
  parallel_chains = chains,
  init = inits,
  iter_sampling = samples,
  iter_warmup = warmup,
  save_warmup = TRUE,
  seed = md$seed
)

# save fitted model to disk
fit$save_object(file = file.path(wd, "fit.rds"))

title: Practical Tutorial: Posteriors, Likelihoods, and Priors
text:
Uninformative Prior
Now, we are ready to plot the likelihood and prior alongside the posterior distribution. We will focus on the mean parameter \(\mu\) from our model.

myplot(
  fit = fit,
  md = md,
  par = "mu",
  xlim = c(3, 7), # lower and upper x-axis values for the plot
  prior_mean = 0, # this should match the mean of the prior on mu in model_of_the_mean.stan
  prior_sd = 1000 # match the sd of the prior on mu in model_of_the_mean.stan
)








Remember that we set an uninformative prior on the \(\mu\) parameter in our model (i.e. \(\mu \sim normal(0, 100)\)), so it appears as a flat line at the bottom of this plot. Notice that our Bayesian posterior is essentially equivalent to the likelihood in this case because the prior is uninformative.






Note



Likelihoods are not probabilities (i.e. they do not range from zero to one and they do not sum to one across all possible outcomes). We have rescaled our likelihood to have the same height as our posterior just so that we can plot them together.

title: Practical Tutorial: Posteriors, Likelihoods, and Priors
section: Informative Prior Aligned With True Parameter Value
text:
Informative Prior Aligned With True Parameter Value
Now, let’s test a strongly informative prior that is well aligned with the data signal. Here we will use the prior \(\mu \sim normal(5, 0.1)\) (remember, 5 is our true population mean that we defined to generate our simulated data). We are using the exact same simulated dataset and initial values from our original model.









 We can see the the posterior now has less uncertainty (i.e. less variance) than the likelihood. Why is that?
 Is our posterior well aligned with our likelihood? What are some reasonable scenarios when the posterior would differ from the likelihood under these conditions?

title: Practical Tutorial: Posteriors, Likelihoods, and Priors
section: Informative Prior Not Aligned With True Parameter Value
text:
Informative Prior Not Aligned With True Parameter Value
Now, let’s test a strongly informative prior that is not well aligned with the true parameter value. In other words, our prior is strong and wrong (a bad combo)! Here we will use the prior \(\mu \sim normal(4, 0.1)\) (remember, 5 is our true population mean that we defined to generate our simulated data). We are using the exact same simulated dataset and initial values from our original model.









 Our posterior now falls somewhere between the prior and the likelihood. Why is that?
 What do you think would happen if the prior was slightly less informative (e.g. slightly more variance in the prior)? Can you test that?

title: Practical Tutorial: Gaussian Linear Regression
text: Now that we can design and run a Bayesian model of the mean, let’s add a deterministic linear regression on the mean.

title: Practical Tutorial: Gaussian Linear Regression
text:
data
The data model block now includes an integer K that defines the number of predictor variables and a matrix \(x_{i,k}\) of values for our predictors. Notice that this matrix has a row for each sample n and a column for each predictor variable \(k\).

title: Practical Tutorial: Gaussian Linear Regression
text:
parameters
The parameters block now includes our regression coefficients: the intercept alpha (\(\alpha\)) and the effect size beta (\(\beta\)) of each predictor variable.

title: Practical Tutorial: Gaussian Linear Regression
text:
transformed parameters
This model block was not included in our model of the mean. This is where we can define parameters that are derived deterministically from other parameters and data in the model. In this case, our linear regression determines the mean \(\mu\) of the normal distribution used as our likelihood in the model{} block below.
Note that we are using a matrix multiplication to multiply the matrix \(x_{i,k}\) of predictor variables by our vector of regression coefficients \(\beta_k\). This notation provides flexibility to include more (or fewer) predictor variables in the model by simply modifying the data and without needing to rewrite the model code.

title: Practical Tutorial: Gaussian Linear Regression
text:
model
This block is very similar to our model of the mean. The difference is only that mu (\(\mu\)) is now derived in the transformed parameters block rather than having a prior in the model block, and we have added priors for alpha (\(\alpha\)) and beta (\(\beta\)).
We have introduced a new distribution as the prior for the standard deviation sigma (\(\sigma\)) in our likelihood. This is the half-cauchy distribution (“half” because sigma is defined to be greater than 0 in the parameters block). The Cauchy distribution is a t-distribution with one degree of freedom. This is similar to a normal distribution with “fat” tails (i.e. a higher probability of outliers). This is commonly used as the prior for standard deviation parameters, although there are other viable alternatives (e.g. uniform, half-normal).

title: Practical Tutorial: Gaussian Linear Regression
text:
Model Diagnostics
Let’s start by looking at our traceplots.

# traceplots to visually inspect MCMC chains
bayesplot::mcmc_trace(
  fit$draws(),
  pars = c(
    "alpha",
    paste0("beta[", 1:md$K, "]"),
    "sigma"
  )
)








 What do you think? Do we have convergence?
If the traceplots visually appear converged and there are no obvious issues, let’s formally confirm convergence for each parameter with the r-hat statistics (i.e. we’re looking for r-hat < 1.01 for publication quality convergence or r-hat < 1.1 for a reliable exploratory model).

# Check r-hat for convergence
posterior::rhat(fit$draws("alpha"))

[1] 1.000035

posterior::rhat(fit$draws("beta[1]"))

[1] 1.000847

posterior::rhat(fit$draws("beta[2]"))

[1] 0.9999446

posterior::rhat(fit$draws("sigma"))

[1] 0.9999163


 Are all of our parameters converged?

title: Practical Tutorial: Gaussian Linear Regression
Practical Tutorial: Gaussian Linear Regression
text:
R Analysis
gaussian_linear_regression.R

# cleanup
rm(list = ls())
gc()
cat("\014")
try(dev.off(), silent = T)

# check working directory
getwd()

# [optional] update/fix working directory
# setwd(file.path('/my/working/directory/model_of_the_mean'))

# directories
wd <- getwd()
dir.create(wd, showWarnings = F, recursive = T)

# load libraries
library(cmdstanr)
library(posterior)
library(bayesplot)

# set seed for random number generators (important for reproducibility)
seed <- round(runif(1, 1, 1e6))
set.seed(seed)

#---- simulate data (Gaussian) ----#

# define the sample size
n <- 1e3

# number of covariates (use K > 1)
K <- 2
if (K < 2) {
  stop("Please define K as 2 or more.")
}

# create covariates
x <- matrix(NA, nrow = n, ncol = K)
for (k in 1:K) {
  x[, k] <- rnorm(n, 0, 1)
}

# define regression parameters (randomly)
alpha <- rnorm(1, 0, 1)
beta <- rnorm(K, 0, 3)
sigma <- runif(1, 0, 2)

# generate response variable
y <- alpha + as.vector(x %*% beta) + rnorm(n, 0, sigma)

# note: %*% is a matrix multiplication of a matrix of x values times a vector of beta values
# convince yourself that (x %*% beta) is equal to (beta1 * x1 + beta2 * x2)
head(x[, 1:2] %*% beta[1:2])
head(beta[1] * x[, 1] + beta[2] * x[, 2])

# visualise covariate relationships with response variable
plot(y ~ x[, 1])
plot(y ~ x[, 2])

# summary statistics of response variable
summary(y)

# density plot of response variable
plot(density(y))
rug(y)

#---- run Bayesian model (CmdStandR) ----#

# format data as a list (required by stan)
md <- list(
  n = n,
  K = K,
  y = as.vector(y),
  x = x,
  alpha_true = alpha,
  beta_true = beta,
  sigma_true = sigma,
  seed = seed # important to set and save seed for reproducibility
)

# save data to disk
saveRDS(
  object = md,
  file = file.path(wd, "md.rds")
)


# define location of the stan model file
model_file <- file.path(wd, "gaussian_linear_regression.stan")

# compile the stan model
mod <- cmdstan_model(model_file)


# function to generate initial values for each parameter in the model
init_generator <- function(md = md, chain_id = 1) {
  result <- list()

  result[["alpha"]] <- runif(1, -10, 10)
  result[["beta"]] <- runif(md$K, -10, 10)
  result[["sigma"]] <- runif(1, 0, 1e2)

  return(result)
}


# MCMC config
chains <- 4
warmup <- 1e3
samples <- 2e3
inits <- lapply(1:chains, function(id) init_generator(md = md, chain_id = id))

# run MCMC
fit <- mod$sample(
  data = md,
  parallel_chains = chains,
  init = inits,
  iter_sampling = samples,
  iter_warmup = warmup,
  save_warmup = TRUE,
  seed = md$seed
)

# save model to disk
fit$save_object(file = file.path(wd, "fit.rds"))

# traceplots to visually inspect MCMC chains
bayesplot::mcmc_trace(
  fit$draws(),
  pars = c(
    "alpha",
    paste0("beta[", 1:md$K, "]"),
    "sigma"
  )
)

# Check r-hat for convergence
posterior::rhat(fit$draws("alpha"))
posterior::rhat(fit$draws("beta[1]"))
posterior::rhat(fit$draws("beta[2]"))
posterior::rhat(fit$draws("sigma"))

# parameters from the true unobserved population (i.e. from simulation)
alpha
beta
sigma

# summary of model results
pars <- c("alpha", "beta", "sigma")
fit$summary(variables = pars)

# visualise marginal posterior distributions for parameters as density plots
pars <- c("alpha", paste0("beta[", 1:md$K, "]"), "sigma")
bayesplot::mcmc_areas(fit$draws(), pars = pars, prob = 0.95)

# ... as histograms
bayesplot::mcmc_hist(fit$draws(), pars = pars)

title: Lecture Slides: GLM and Hierarchical Models

title: Humanitarian population nowcasting
text:
We contribute to international humanitarian response using digital traces and remote sensing for population nowcasting–near real-time population estimation.
Our work in this area began in the immediate aftermath of the large-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine on the 22 February 2022 when we teamed up with the UN International Organization for Migration to repurpose targeted advertising data from social media into a tool for targeted humanitarian aid (Leasure et al. 2023). We later transferred these approaches to Gaza supporting the UN Office for Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs and the Site Management Cluster (Acted and IOM). You can read about some of our early work for Gaza from Darin et al. (2026) that further developed these methods and data to provide a generalised toolbox for digital traces in crisis response.
Since our initial work with social media targeted advertising data in Ukraine and Gaza, the data landscape has unsurprisingly changed in both of these crises, and we have been continuously working on methods that can help the humanitarian responses adapt to these changes. This has included Bayesian mark-recapture methods to leverage polio vaccination data for estimation of child population sizes and vaccine coverage in Gaza, using Vodafone advertising data to estimate internal (sub-national) population flows in Ukraine, demographic indirect estimation using privacy-preserving telecommunications data for population nowcasting, and machine learning for automated tent mapping from satellite imagery.
Our aim with this collection of tutorials and documentation is to make these methods more accessible to you. We will walk you through some of the details and provide the source code so that you can reproduce and adapt the methods yourself. This is part of our vision for open-source innovation for humanitarian population nowcasting so that science can be harnessed and adapted more quickly to respond to crisis events. We hope you find these materials useful in your own work and that we can grow the community of researchers working together to improve these approaches.

title: Gaza NowPop - Telecoms
text:
Introduction
As we carry our cellphones around in our pockets, they are silently pinging nearby cell towers to maintain a connection with the network. Working with the United Nations Office for Coordination Affairs (UNOCHA) to provide up-to-date demographic data for humanitarian needs assessments, we use anonymised and aggregated counts of users on each tower in the Gaza strip across two mobile phone networks to provide snapshot counts of mobile phone users in the general vicinity of each tower. These data contain no information about individual people or their specific locations.
Our goal is to utilise this information to estimate population sizes on a 100-m grid by incorporating additional information about the locations of tent shelters and undamaged housing units inside buildings. Because these data do not include information about people without cell phones, we need to account for mobile network coverage to scale up from mobile phone users to total population.






NoteOpen-source



The source code for this analysis pipeline is publicly available from GitHub with an open-source license: https://github.com/realgoodresearch/GazaNowPop.
Check the ./src/deterministic/ folder with sourcecode for the “deterministic” pipeline described here. Note: We are also pursuing a Bayesian statistical approach in the repository that is not yet production-ready.

title: Gaza NowPop - Telecoms
text:
Data
The primary data used in this pipeline are:

Telecommunications - Aggregated and anonymised counts of active subscribers on each geolocated telecommunications tower from two mobile network operators in the Gaza Strip (UNOCHA, personal communication).
Housing Units - Comprehensive building damage assessment from UNOSAT (UNOSAT 2025).

Additional attributes were requested from UNOSAT to represent estimates of undamaged housing units in each building (UNOSAT, personal communication).

Tents - Maps of tent point locations have been obtained from two sources depending on the date;

Real Good Research TentNetFA automated tent mapping (e.g. Zhang et al. 2026).
UNOSAT manual tent mapping (not publicly available).


Additional data that are utilised include:

Administrative boundaries - Governorates, municipalities, and neighbourhoods (UNOCHA, personal communication)
Yellow-line militarised area - The boundaries of the IDF-enforced yellow line that excludes civilians from entering (UNOCHA, personal communication). We exclude areas behind the yellow line from our analyses.

Evacuation orders - For dates up to 13 September 2025, we utilised Israeli military displacement orders (UNOCHA 2025).

title: Gaza NowPop - Telecoms
text:
Analysis
Let’s begin with a quick overview of the phases of the analysis pipeline, and then we’ll dive into each one in a little more detail.
We first estimate the geographic area that each telecommunications tower covers. Within each of these catchment areas, we allocate subscribers from the tower into 100-m grid cells based on the availability of shelters in each grid cell. The shelters could be tents or undamaged housing units in buildings. This results in a 100-m grid of subscriber counts for each of the two mobile networks. We combine these subscriber grids and scale up to total population–including the sub-population not active on either network–based on the penetration rates of each mobile network. The calculations of penetration rates assume that the total population size for the Gaza strip is 2.13-million people (PCBS 2025), and our population estimates always sum up to match this number.

Tower catchment areas
We do not know the exact coverage area of each telecommunications tower. We implement a very simple approach to approximate tower catchment areas by assuming that each phone connects to the nearest tower within 2-km. We chose 2-km as a rough estimate of the maximum coverage radius for a 2G tower. Estimating tower catchment areas could include significant detail including signal attenuation curves, effects of topography, and buildings. However, this is not required for our purposes, and we did not have sufficient information to build a well parameterised coverage model.
We use Voronoi polygons with a 2-km clip radius to enforece a maximum signal distance. We calculate these simple tower catchment areas separately for each mobile network (Figure 1).






Figure 1: Example of mobile tower catchment areas estimated using Voronoi polygons. Red represents mobile network operator #1 and blue represents mobile network operator #2. Note: These are synthetic tower locations used for illustration purposes only.



We have a count of users on each tower, and we assume that they are located somewhere within the catchment polygon. Our next objective is to logically distribute users among potential locations within each tower catchment area.


Available dwellings
Mobile phone users that have been counted on a tower are likely to be located in a building or tent within the tower’s catchment area. Our next step is to quantify tents and undamaged housing units within 100-m grid cells to help us allocate users from a tower into grid cells within its catchment area.

Tents
We use a map of tent locations covering the Gaza strip. UNOSAT has produced manually validated tent maps for some dates, but for other dates we use our own automated tent maps extracted from Planet Labs satellite imagery using the open-source TentNetFA algorithm (Figure 2).





  
    
    
    
    ⛶
  




Figure 2: Move the slider to show/hide tent points to visually compare with the underlying satellite imagery. Click the fullscreen button to enlarge the comparison.





Housing units
Some populations are living inside buildings, and we need to map those available shelter locations as well. The challenge is the widespread destruction of buildings in the Gaza strip. We have relied on the Comprehensive Damage Assessments from UNOSAT (UNOSAT 2025; Figure 3) which were appended upon request by UNOSAT with estimates of undamaged housing units in each building. The building locations and original number of housing units are based on the PCBS cadastral registry, which UNOSAT updated based on their satellite-based assessment of building damage.






Figure 3: UNOSAT building damage assessments showing the data categories: red=destroyed; orange=severely damaged; yellow=moderately damaged; green=possibly damaged; teal=no visible damage; blue=possible damage from adjacent impact, debris.





Dwelling grids
Tents and undamaged housing units are combined into a 100-m grid that includes the count of available dwellings (tents or housing units) in each grid cell (Figure 4).






Figure 4: 100-m gridded count of available dwellings. The count includes tents and individual undamaged housing units inside buildings.






Subscriber grids
We can now allocate users from each tower into dwellings within the catchment area of the tower. This is done by calculating the average number of mobile phone subscribers per available shelter in the catchment area for a tower and then allocating equal numbers of subscribers into each dwelling (Figure 5). This process assumes homogeneous household sizes in every tent and housing unit and that all dwellings are occupied. These assumptions are necessary given the data available and should be taken into account upon interpretation of the results.






Figure 5: 100-m gridded counts of mobile phone subscribers on each network.





Population estimation
The subscriber grids count active mobile subscribers, not people. We therefore convert subscriber counts to population estimates while allowing for people without an active phone on either network.
First, we split the study area into cells with coverage from at least one provider and cells with no provider coverage. Let (T = 2,130,000) be the assumed total population, (H) the number of available dwellings in the covered area, and (J) the number in the uncovered area. We use the average number of people per available dwelling,
\[
\phi = \frac{T}{H + J},
\]
to estimate the population in the covered area, \(N = H\phi\), and the population outside coverage, \(M = J\phi\). This provides the population denominator needed for the mobile-network calculations.
For each provider (k), its penetration rate within the covered area is the total number of subscribers allocated to its grid, divided by (N):
\[
p_k = \frac{\sum_g S_{k,g}}{N},
\]
where \(S_{k,g}\) is the estimated number of active subscribers of provider (k) in grid cell (g). Intuitively, \(p_k\) is the estimated share of people in the covered area who appear as active subscribers on that network. The rates are calculated separately for the two providers.
We then estimate the population of each 100-m grid cell according to which networks cover it. For a cell with no network coverage, we use the dwelling-based estimate. For a cell covered by only provider 1 or only provider 2, we divide that provider’s subscriber count by its penetration rate. Where both providers have coverage, we combine their subscriber counts and their penetration rates:
\[
\widehat{P}_g =
\begin{cases}
D_g\phi, & \text{no provider coverage}, \\
S_{1,g}/p_1, & \text{provider 1 only}, \\
S_{2,g}/p_2, & \text{provider 2 only}, \\
\left(S_{1,g} + S_{2,g}\right) / \left(p_1 + p_2\right), & \text{both providers},
\end{cases}
\]
where \(D_g\) is the number of available dwellings in 100-m grid cell (g). Finally, we rescale every grid-cell estimate by the same factor so that the full population grid sums exactly to (T). This corrects small differences introduced by coverage boundaries, missing cells, and raster calculations while preserving the relative pattern of the estimates.

Population per dwelling type
To separate the resulting population into people living in tents and people living in buildings, we calculate a cell-specific average household size:
\[
h_g = \frac{\widehat{P}_g}{A_g + B_g},
\]
where \(A_g\) is the number of tents and \(B_g\) is the number of undamaged housing units in buildings. The corresponding estimates are
\[
\widehat{P}^{\mathrm{tent}}_g = A_g h_g
\qquad \text{and} \qquad
\widehat{P}^{\mathrm{building}}_g = B_g h_g.
\]
By construction, these two estimates sum to the total population estimate in each cell.
This approach makes several explicit assumptions:

Every available tent and undamaged housing unit is occupied.
Within a cell, tents and housing units have the same average household size.
The penetration rate for each provider is constant throughout its coverage area.
Subscriber counts from the two providers represent distinct network memberships; the combined-rate calculation does not correct for people who hold active subscriptions on both networks.
The assumed Gaza-wide total population of 2.13 million is correct for the reference date.

At this point, we have population estimates on a 100-m grid for every grid cell with available dwellings according to our tent and building maps, excluding areas within the yellow line exclusion zone.






Figure 6: 100-m gridded population estimates.






Aggregation
The 100-m gridded population estimates are primarily intended as a geographical unit of analysis to facilitate flexibility aggregating population estimates for larger areas. Due to the various assumptions that we have highlighted, we do not expect the population estimates to be precise at the level of individual 100-m grid cells. We expect the estimates to be more reliable at larger aggregated spatial scales. We provide such aggregations for neighbourhoods (Figure 7), municipalities, and governorates. We also provide the 100-m gridded estimates so that partners can aggregate to other spatial units (e.g. site boundaries or healthcare catchment areas).






Figure 7: Population estimates aggregated to neighbourhoods.

title: Gaza NowPop - Telecoms
text:
Triangulation
There are no reliable validation datasets available for assessing accuracy of these population estimates. The best that we can do is to triangulate the estimates with other sources of information from the field. This is coordinated through partnerships with UNOCHA and the Site Management Cluster. When discrepencies are found, we investigate the underlying causes and work to improve the methodology through these investigations.
We have experimented with a Bayesian statistical approach that could replace the deterministic estimation described here. One advantage (out of many) of a statistical approach is the ability to conduct out-of-sample cross-validation in which telecommunications data could be witheld from model fitting and used to assess prediction accuracy. The deterministic approach described here is ideal for rapid-response operational population estimation, while we continue to pursue a robust statistical method suitable for this data landscape in parallel.

title: Gaza NowPop - Telecoms
text:
Assumptions and Limitations

We assume that mobile phones connect to the nearest tower within 2-km rather than pursuing a more advanced tower coverage model.

Our automated tent maps (and even manually-produced tent maps) are known to include errors (i.e. false positive and false negatives). We are working on pipelines to efficiently generate validation and training data for continuous improvements.

We assume that every available tent and undamaged housing unit is occupied, although some at very low population densities.
Within a cell, we assume that tents and housing units have the same average household size, but this household size can vary among cells.
The penetration rate for each provider is assumed to be constant throughout its coverage area, which is necessary without additional information.
Subscriber counts from the two providers represent distinct network memberships; we do not correct for people who hold active subscriptions on both networks.
The assumed Gaza-wide total population of 2.13 million is correct for the reference date.

title: Ukraine NowPop - Telecoms advertising data
text:
Introduction
Since the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, millions of people have left the country, moved within it, and, increasingly, returned. Humanitarian planning needs up-to-date answers to three questions: how many people live in each community now, who they are by age and sex, and where they have come from. Ukraine has had no census since 2001, and conventional population estimates cannot keep pace with displacement on this scale.
Mobile networks observe these movements continuously. Unlike our Gaza NowPop work, which uses counts of users connected to individual cell towers, here we use a commercial data product: aggregated statistics that a mobile network operator in Ukraine produces for targeted marketing purposes and makes available for purchase. Using an off-the-shelf data product has practical advantages: it can be bought through a standard commercial process, it arrives already aggregated at administrative level, and it comes in a regular format with age and sex. The trade-off is that we cannot control how the aggregates are produced, and that keeping estimates up to date means continuing to buy data updates.
Telecom advertising data were not our first exercise. Our earlier nowcasts for Ukraine used social media advertising audience counts from Meta (Leasure et al. 2023), but a change to Meta’s Marketing API in May 2024 made those data unsuitable on their own for real-time nowcasting. We therefore moved to telecom advertising data, which offered something new: as well as counting subscribers in each place, they record, for each pair of locations, how many subscribers moved between locations. These monthly flows let us better track how the share of residents on the network, the penetration rate, changes over time and space as people move.
Our modelling goal is to convert monthly subscriber flows into monthly population estimates and population flows for each hromada (Ukraine’s basic municipal unit), by age group and sex, consistent with the national population after accounting for people who have crossed the border.
This work was undertaken at the Demographic Science Unit, University of Oxford, in partnership with the World Health Organization (WHO) Ukraine.






NoteOpen-source



The source code for this analysis pipeline is publicly available from GitHub with an open-source license (GPL-3.0): https://github.com/OxfordDemSci/UkraineNowPop.
The method described here is in the ./src/analysis/ folder, and the data preparation in ./src/data_prep/.

title: Ukraine NowPop - Telecoms advertising data
text:
Data
The primary data used in this pipeline are:

Telecom subscribers flows - A commercial data product from a mobile phone company in Ukraine, designed for advertising, giving aggregated monthly counts of subscribers by age group and sex. A subscriber’s home hromada is their most common night-time location over the previous three months. We use three of the product’s tables:

Monthly flows: subscribers whose home hromada last month was \(i\) and whose current home hromada is \(j\). Besides hromadas, origins can be Abroad (subscribers returning from outside Ukraine) or Unknown (subscribers whose previous location is not known, such as new subscribers), and destinations can be Abroad. Monthly flows are only available for government-controlled territory (GCT).
Baseline flows: subscribers whose home hromada in January 2022 was \(i\) and whose current home hromada is \(j\). We use them to account for non-government-controlled territory (NGCT) (see Step 3).
Stocks: subscribers whose home is in each hromada.

Our estimates cover February 2022 to November 2025 for the 18 to 64 years old.
Baseline population - Total population of each hromada in 2022 from the State Statistics Service of Ukraine (SSSU).
Baseline age-sex structure - Population by age and sex for each oblast (region) on 1 January 2022, from the Common Operational Dataset on Population Statistics (COD-PS) for Ukraine (UNFPA, HDX).
Border crossings - Counts of people leaving and entering Ukraine, recorded by the border authorities and published by UNHCR: daily until December 2024, then monthly (UNHCR Operational Data Portal).
Age-sex profile of people leaving - Ukrainians with temporary protection status in neighbouring countries (Hungary, Moldova, Poland, Romania, and Slovakia), by age and sex (Eurostat).
Age-sex profile of people returning - Profiles of returnees from the International Organization for Migration (IOM) Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) Crossing back surveys (IOM DTM). These surveys stopped in December 2024.

Additional data that are used include:

Administrative boundaries - Oblasts, raions (districts), and hromadas with their P-codes from the Common Operational Dataset on Administrative Boundaries (COD-AB) (OCHA, HDX). We also group oblasts into macroregions.
Areas outside government control - We follow the telecom operator’s own classification which is fixed over time.

title: Ukraine NowPop - Telecoms advertising data
text:
Analysis

Data preparation
Some hromadas are missing from the monthly flows for some months. If a hromada is missing for three or fewer consecutive months, we fill the gap by repeating the flows into it from the last month observed before the gap. Hromadas missing for more than three consecutive months are excluded, both as origins and as destinations. 3 hromadas were imputed in this way, and 1,138 hromadas were included in the estimates.


Overview
The pipeline runs month by month. In outline (Figure 1):

Population totals. For each hromada, we measure the penetration rate: the number of the operator’s subscribers per resident. We estimate it at the start of the series, before the full-scale invasion, using the 2022 baseline population. We use it to turn each month’s subscriber flows into population flows, and then update it from the newly estimated population.
Age and sex. We repeat the same logic separately for each age-sex group, at the coarser level of macroregions, where data are more complete. We use the result to split each hromada flow by age and sex.
National consistency. We rescale the estimates so that, for each age-sex group, they match the national population after accounting for cumulative border crossings and the population in non-government-controlled territory (NGCT). This also allows to take into accout change in penetration rate that are affecting uniformly the country.

Summing the estimated flows by destination gives the population of each hromada at each month.

Notation








Indices

Parameters

The first month, \(t_0\), is February 2022, which reflects home locations before the full-scale invasion. The baseline population by age and sex, \(T^C_{t_0,i,a,s}\), is the 2022 total population of hromada \(i\) multiplied by the age-sex proportion \(\pi^O_{t_0,o_i,a,s}\) of its oblast; \(T^C_{t_0,i} = \sum_{a,s} T^C_{t_0,i,a,s}\) is its sum over the age-sex groups covered by the model (18 to 64).


Step 1: Population flows

Initial penetration rate
At \(t_0\), the penetration rate of hromada \(i\) is the number of subscribers whose flows start there, divided by its baseline population:
\[
p_{t_0,i} = \frac{\sum_j S_{t_0,i,j}}{T^C_{t_0,i}}.
\]
The penetration rate captures the operator’s local market share and any differences between subscribers and residents, such as people with more than one SIM card or no phone. Rates are not capped, so a hromada can have more subscribers than residents.


From subscriber flows to population flows
Each month, we divide subscriber flows by the penetration rate of the place they came from, using the rate estimated for the previous month:
\[
\dot N_{t,i,j} =
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{S_{t,i,j}}{p_{t-1,i}}, & \text{origin } i \text{ is a hromada}, \\[2ex]
\dfrac{S_{t,\text{unknown},j}}{p_{t-1,j}}, & \text{origin } i \text{ is Unknown}, \\[2ex]
S_{t,\text{abroad},j}\,\dfrac{BC^{in}_t}{\sum_{j} S_{t,\text{abroad},j}}, & \text{origin }i \text{ is Abroad}.
\end{cases}
\]
Subscribers from an unknown origin take the penetration rate of their destination; if they are going abroad, they take the mean penetration rate. Subscribers arriving from abroad are calibrated directly to the border crossing data: their total equals the number of people recorded entering Ukraine that month, distributed across destinations in proportion to the operator’s returning subscribers. Unlike hromada penetration rates, which are updated from the previous month’s estimates, the rate for arrivals from abroad is reset each month from that month’s border entries.


Updating the penetration rate
Penetration rates change over time because people move, and because the operator’s market share among people who moved can differ from that of people who stayed. After rescaling (Step 3), we update each hromada’s penetration rate as the ratio between the subscribers who were in it and the estimated population there:
\[
p_{t,j} = \frac{\sum_i S_{t,i,j}}{\sum_i N_{t,i,j}}.
\]
This rate is used as the origin penetration rate for flows leaving hromada \(j\) in the following month.



Step 2: Age and sex
Subscriber counts by age and sex are sparse at the hromada level: many age-sex groups have no recorded flows between particular hromadas. We therefore estimate age-sex penetration rates for macroregions:
\[
p_{t_0,m,a,s} = \frac{\sum_{i \in m} \sum_j S_{t_0,i,j,a,s}}{\sum_{i \in m} T^C_{t_0,i,a,s}},
\]
For each month, we compute age-sex specific intermediate flows \(S_{t,i,j,a,s} / p_{t-1,m_i,a,s}\), and from these the age-sex composition \(\pi_{t,a,s}\) of the flows between each pair of origin and destination macroregions. We then split each hromada-level flow from Step 1 according to that composition:
\[
\dot N_{t,i,j,a,s} = \pi_{t,a,s, m_i, m_j}\; \dot N_{t,i,j}.
\]
The total size of each flow therefore comes from the hromada-level penetration rates, while its age-sex composition comes from the macroregion-level rates. For flows from abroad, the age-sex rates are calibrated to border crossings by age and sex (see below). After rescaling, the macroregion age-sex penetration rates are updated in the same way as in Step 1:
\[
p_{t,m,a,s} = \frac{\sum_{j \in m} \sum_i S_{t,i,j,a,s}}{\sum_{j \in m} \sum_i N_{t,i,j,a,s}}.
\]


Step 3: Rescaling to national totals
Step 3 anchor the estimates to an independent national total, built from the baseline population and border crossings, and use the subscriber data ultimately to distribute it across hromadas.

Border crossings by age and sex
Border crossing counts are not broken down by age or sex. We apply the age-sex profile of people under temporary protection in the European Union to departures, and the IOM DTM returnee profile to arrivals:
\[
BC^{out}_{t,a,s} = BC^{out}_t\, \pi^E_{t,a,s},
\qquad
BC^{in}_{t,a,s} = BC^{in}_t\, \pi^{DTM}_{t,a,s}.
\]
The DTM profile uses a broad adult age band; we split it into the model’s age groups using the Eurostat age distribution. When the latest month of border crossing or Eurostat data is not yet available, we carry the most recent values forward.


Population in non-government-controlled territory
The telecom data have limited coverage in non-government-controlled territory: we have only monthly baseline flows which is the number of people that used to be in the NGCT, that are now in the GCT. We estimate the number of subscribers who remain in NGCT as the NGCT subscriber stock minus the baseline flows of subscribers who have left NGCT since before the full-scale invasion:
\[
S_{t,\text{NGCT},\text{NGCT},a,s} = S^{\text{stock}}_{t_0,\text{NGCT},a,s} - S^{BF}_{t,\text{NGCT}, \text{GCT},a,s}.
\]
We convert this to population using the penetration rate at \(t_0\), which we hold constant:
\[
p_{t_0,\text{NGCT},a,s} = \frac{S^{\text{stock}}_{t_0,\text{NGCT},a,s}}{\sum_{i \in \text{NGCT}} T^C_{t_0,i,a,s}},
\qquad
N_{t,\text{NGCT},a,s} = \frac{S_{t,\text{NGCT},\text{NGCT},a,s}}{p_{t_0,\text{NGCT},a,s}}.
\]
These estimates are important to correct the national total used to calibrate the population estimates in the government controlled territory.


National totals and scaling factor
For each age-sex group, the national total in government-controlled territory is the baseline population, minus everyone who has left Ukraine since \(t_0\), plus everyone who has returned, minus the population in non-government-controlled territory:
\[
T^{\text{GCT}}_{t,a,s} = \sum_i T^C_{t_0,i,a,s} \;-\; \sum_{\tau \le t} BC^{out}_{\tau,a,s} \;+\; \sum_{\tau \le t} BC^{in}_{\tau,a,s} \;-\; N_{t,\text{NGCT},\text{NGCT},a,s},
\]
where the baseline sum covers the hromadas in the telecom data and in non-government-controlled territory.
The domestic flows (from one hromada to another) should add up to this total, except for this month’s border crossings, which are represented separately by the flows to and from Abroad. The scaling factor is therefore:
\[
\theta^{-1}_{t,a,s} = \frac{\sum_{i \ne \text{abroad}} \sum_{j \ne \text{abroad}} \dot N_{t,i,j,a,s}}{T^{\text{GCT}}_{t,a,s}}.
\]
The final flows are:
\[
N_{t,i,j,a,s} =
\begin{cases}
\dot N_{t,i,j,a,s}\; \theta_{t,a,s}, & i, j \ne \text{abroad}, \\[1ex]
\dot N_{t,i,\text{abroad},a,s}\; \dfrac{BC^{out}_{t,a,s}}{\sum_{i} \dot N_{t,i,\text{abroad},a,s}}, & j = \text{abroad}, \\[2ex]
\dot N_{t,\text{abroad},j,a,s}, & i = \text{abroad}.
\end{cases}
\]
Flows to Abroad are rescaled so that they sum to the number of people recorded leaving Ukraine that month. Flows from Abroad are already calibrated to arrivals and are not rescaled. Subscribers recorded as moving from abroad to abroad are dropped, because they cannot be calibrated.
Putting the three steps together, each domestic estimate is a subscriber count multiplied by an inverse penetration rate, an age-sex proportion, and a national scaling factor:
\[
N_{t,i,j,a,s} = S_{t,i,j}\; p^{-1}_{t-1,i}\; \pi_{t,a,s, m_i,m_j}\; \theta_{t,a,s}.
\]



Outputs

Population count at hromada level
The population of hromada \(j\) in month \(t\) is the sum of all flows arriving there:
\[
N_{t,j,a,s} = \sum_i N_{t,i,j,a,s}.
\]



Population estimates at the hromada-level for November 2025 showing the hromadas for which telecom data were available to support up-to-date population estimation.




Population monthly timeserie from February 2022 to November 2025



Monthly population trends through time for all hromadas included in the telecom analysis for each oblast. Note that the count of hromadas included for each oblast is listed under the oblast name at the top of each panel.




Population from and to abroad



Number of people estimated to be moving to Ukraine from abroad (left) or moving abroad from Ukraine (right) for each hromada in November 2025.




Age and sex compositional shift



Change in the age-sex composition of populations in the hromadas that experience the largest change between October and November 2025.


We release one pair of CSV files per month:

Population stocks - estimated population in each hromada.
Population flows - estimated number of people whose home was in one hromada last month and in another (or the same) hromada this month, including flows to and from Abroad and from Unknown origins.

Each row identifies the hromada, raion, and oblast by COD P-code, with names in English and Ukrainian. Columns give estimates for each sex (F, M, or total T) and age group (18_24, 25_34, 35_44, 45_54, 55_64, or all adults 18_64); for example, F_18_24 holds women aged 18 to 24.
As with any small-area estimate, individual hromada figures are less reliable than aggregates. We recommend aggregating to raions or oblasts where possible.
The estimates are classified as restricted with moderate sensitivity, following the OCHA Information Sharing Protocol for Ukraine. They can be explored in the Ukraine NowPop dashboard, which shows population estimates for a chosen month, age-sex group, and geographic level, as well as flows between areas. Oblast-level results are public; raion- and hromada-level results require user authentication.

title: Ukraine NowPop - Telecoms advertising data
text:
Triangulation
There is no complete, independent count of Ukraine’s population after February 2022 against which to validate these estimates. We compare them with other sources:

Official population estimates - We compare our estimates with the 2023, 2024, and 2025 COD-PS updates produced by the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), by age and sex, at national and oblast level, and map the differences. To make the comparison fair, we restrict it to raions in which every hromada is covered by the telecom data.
Displacement surveys - We compare estimated internal movements with the numbers of internally displaced people (IDPs) reported by the IOM DTM, for each oblast and month.

The relative age structure of our estimates aligns closely with COD-PS in every year, particularly in the middle working-age groups. However, our estimates suggest fewer women than COD-PS in most age groups. This may be because our method accounts for flows to and from abroad by age and sex, using the border crossing data.

Our estimates of internal movement follow the same trends as the IDP numbers reported by IOM, but are about 15 times larger. This is expected because the two measure different things: IOM counts internally displaced people, whereas we count every change of home hromada. The discrepancy was much larger during the first few months after the full-scale invasion, which may reflect both this difference in definitions and reporting errors during that chaotic period.
Because the telecom data are updated monthly, the estimates can complement the annual COD-PS updates between releases.
The method described here is a rapid-response approach designed to deliver operational estimates quickly from a single data source. In parallel, we are developing a Bayesian statistical framework that integrates several data sources, so that estimates remain stable when any one source changes or is lost.

title: Ukraine NowPop - Telecoms advertising data
text:
Assumptions and limitations

Coverage. Estimates are only produced for hromadas with consistent telecom data through time. Crimea, Sevastopol, and Donetska and Luhanska oblasts are not covered, nor are a further 103 hromadas.
Age. Subscriber data are sparse for people under 18 and over 64, so the estimates cover only adults aged 18 to 64.
Home location. A subscriber’s home is their most common night-time location over the previous three months, so the estimates do not capture sudden, short-term moves.
Penetration rates. The initial penetration rate depends on the accuracy of the 2022 baseline population. Updated rates assume that the subscribers in a hromada are representative of its estimated population.
Age and sex. Age-sex penetration rates are assumed to be the same for all hromadas in a macroregion, and the baseline age-sex structure of each oblast is assumed to apply to all its hromadas.
Unknown origins and abroad. Subscribers with an unknown origin are assumed to resemble residents of their destination. Flows to and from abroad rely on border crossing totals and on age-sex profiles from other sources, which may not represent everyone crossing the border: temporary protection beneficiaries in neighbouring countries for departures, and IOM returnee surveys for arrivals. Because those surveys stopped in December 2024, we assume the returnee profile has not changed since.
Non-government-controlled territory. The population there is estimated from very limited data, using a penetration rate held constant since \(t_0\). The baseline flows show people moving from non-government-controlled into government-controlled territory, but we must assume that nobody moves the other way.
Border crossings. Without more detailed information, we assume that every border crossing involves one of the hromadas in the government-controlled territory. We therefore assume no border-crossing from non-government-controlled territory are recorded.
Natural change. The national total is updated only for border crossings. Births, deaths, and ageing since 2022 are not accounted for.
Commercial aggregates. The data are a marketing product, so we do not control or fully observe how subscribers are assigned to hromadas, age groups, and sex. Changes in how the operator produces the product can appear as artificial population changes.
Data continuity. Estimates go out of date unless new data are purchased, and they depend on a single data source.

title: Practical Tutorial: Synthetic Controls
text:
Introduction
Imagine an alternate reality in which Russia’s large scale invasion of Ukraine never happened. Or where the British referendum vote had rejected Brexit. Would global migration patterns look different in these alternate realities?
In this exercise, we will learn how to develop Bayesian synthetic control models to infer migration under these alternative scenarios and compare them to observed migration to asses the effect of these world events.

Background
Synthetic control models are really just a fancy weighted average.
We have a timeseries of observations from our “treated unit” with observations before and after some intervention date. This could be an economic indicator before and after a policy change, for example. We want a model that can estimate what we would have observed in the post-intervention period if there had been no intervention. We do that by taking a weighted average of observations from untreated units in our “donor pool”. The “donors” could be countries where no policy change was introduced.
Estimating the weights is the real trick. We need to find weights for our weighted average that reproduce the pre-intervention observations in the treated country based on observations from the donor countries. These weights are often determined through optimisation algorithms, but we’re going to learn how to estimate them statistically in a Bayesian context. This has some advantages in terms of estimating uncertainty as well as flexibility to specify different models depending on the characteristics of our data.


Traditional synthetic controls
We can see a nice (non-Bayesian) synthetic controls model from the example analysis for the tidysynth R package (see here). The example is based on a study from Abadie et al. (2010) which evaluated the impact that a large-scale tobacco control program in California had on cigarette sales. The model uses cigaratte sales in “donor” states to estimate what the trend would have been in California without the tobacco law.
In the figure below, we can see that the synthetic control predictions in the pre-intervetion period look quite close to reality which gives us confidence that the weighted average is working well. The observed cigarette sales declined significantly compared to the synthetic control in the post-intervention period which indicates to us that the 1988 California law was successful in reducing tobacco sales.


Show the R code
data("smoking")

smoking_out <-
  smoking %>%

  # initial the synthetic control object
  synthetic_control(
    outcome = cigsale, # outcome
    unit = state, # unit index in the panel data
    time = year, # time index in the panel data
    i_unit = "California", # unit where the intervention occurred
    i_time = 1988, # time period when the intervention occurred
    generate_placebos = T # generate placebo synthetic controls (for inference)
  ) %>%

  # Generate the aggregate predictors used to fit the weights

  # average log income, retail price of cigarettes, and proportion of the
  # population between 15 and 24 years of age from 1980 - 1988
  generate_predictor(
    time_window = 1980:1988,
    ln_income = mean(lnincome, na.rm = T),
    ret_price = mean(retprice, na.rm = T),
    youth = mean(age15to24, na.rm = T)
  ) %>%

  # average beer consumption in the donor pool from 1984 - 1988
  generate_predictor(
    time_window = 1984:1988,
    beer_sales = mean(beer, na.rm = T)
  ) %>%

  # Lagged cigarette sales
  generate_predictor(time_window = 1975, cigsale_1975 = cigsale) %>%
  generate_predictor(time_window = 1980, cigsale_1980 = cigsale) %>%
  generate_predictor(time_window = 1988, cigsale_1988 = cigsale) %>%

  # Generate the fitted weights for the synthetic control
  generate_weights(
    optimization_window = 1970:1988, # time to use in the optimization task
    margin_ipop = .02,
    sigf_ipop = 7,
    bound_ipop = 6 # optimizer options
  ) %>%

  # Generate the synthetic control
  generate_control()

# Plotting the result
smoking_out %>% plot_trends()










This example analysis used covariates (age and beer sales) along with lagged effects that we will not explore in our Bayesian synthetic controls, although they could be implemented as extensions to the models we will develop below.

title: Practical Tutorial: Synthetic Controls
text:
A Bayesian analysis: Ukrainian refugees
Now let’s see if we can build our own Bayesian synthetic control model. Here we’ll look at how the Russian invasion of Ukraine on 22 February 2022 affected migration from Ukraine to Germany.

Note: You can easily change the countries and intervation date for the analysis if you want to investigate a different topic (e.g. maybe you want to look at effects of Brexit implementation on 1 January 2021 or some other policy change).


R environment
Before we get started, we have a few quick housekeeping items to get out of the way. In this tutorial, we’re going to need the following R packages:

library(cmdstanr)
library(bayesplot)
library(posterior)
library(tools)
library(tibble)
library(tidyr)
library(tidybayes)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

If you haven’t yet installed cmdstanr, please go back to the Getting Started tutorial.
If you don’t have any of the other R packages, you can install them with this code:


Show the R code
pkgs <- c(
  "tools",
  "bayesplot",
  "posterior",
  "tibble",
  "tidyr",
  "tidybayes",
  "dplyr",
  "ggplot2"
)

pkgs_missing <- setdiff(pkgs, rownames(installed.packages()))
if (length(pkgs_missing) > 0) {
  install.packages(pkgs_missing)
}


Let’s also go ahead and setup our working directory and output directory:

outdir <- file.path(getwd(), "synthetic_controls")
dir.create(outdir, recursive = TRUE)



Raw data
We will be using Meta’s global migration dataset which contains monthly flows of migrants between countries estimated based on where people are when they connect to Facebook and Instagram (Chi et al. 2025). These data are feely available for download from Meta on the Humanitarian Data Exchange.
These data give us counts of migrants that moved from one country to another (including almost all countries globally) during each month from January 2019 to December 2022. A person needs to stay in a country for at least 12 months to be counted as a resident there. The data generating process accounted for differences in social media use to produce a relatively unbiased estimator of migration.
Now we’ll download the data into our working directory and load it into our R environment:

# filename to save the data
dat_filename <- file.path(outdir, "international_migration_flow.csv")

# download the data if we don't already have it
if (!file.exists(dat_filename)) {
  download.file(
    "https://data.humdata.org/dataset/e09595bd-f4c5-4a66-8130-5a05f14d5e64/resource/67b2d6fc-ff4f-4d04-a75e-80e3de81b072/download/international_migration_flow.csv",
    destfile = dat_filename
  )
}

# load the data into R
dat <- read.csv(dat_filename)

So you can get a better idea of what we’re working with, let’s take a quick look at the slice of data where Ukraine (UA) is the origin country:







Note: Countries are identified in the dataset based on their ISO-2 country codes which can be found on Wikipedia.



Poisson model
The basic Bayesian synthetic controls model that we will start with uses a Poisson likelihood since we are dealing with count data.
\[
\begin{aligned}
y_t &\sim Poisson(\lambda_t) \\
\lambda_t &= e^{\alpha} \sum_{k=1}^K w_k x_{k,t} \\
\end{aligned}
\]
where \(y_{t}\) are counts of migrants from Ukraine to Germany each month \(t\) and \(x_{k,t}\) are counts of migrants from each donor country \(k\) to Germany each month. The values of \(x_{k,t}\) have been re-scaled by dividing by the maximum value for each donor \(k\) so that values are comparable across countries and so that the values of \(x_{k,t}\) are always positive.
The weights \(w_k\) for each donor country are parameters that control how much each donor influences the synthetic control (i.e. estimate of alternate reality) for our treatment country. The weights are positive values and must sum to one across all donor countries. So the weighted average is defined as \(\sum_{k=1}^K w_k x_{k,t}\).
The parameter \(\alpha\) is essentially just a scaling factor that rescales our weighted average to match the scale of \(y_t\). For example, if \(\alpha=10\), then it would would scale a weighted average of 1 up to an outcome of 22,000.
We assign minimally informative priors to the parameters.
\[
\begin{aligned}
w_k &\sim Dirichlet(rep(1, K)) \\
\alpha &\sim Normal(0, 10)
\end{aligned}
\]
We chose a \(Normal(0, 10)\) for the prior on \(\alpha\) because the weighted average will always be between zero and one, while the outcome \(y_t\) is on a scale of thousands of migrants.
We chose a Dirichlet prior because it is appropriate for a simplex–a vector of values between zero and one that must sum to one. Setting its parameter to a vector of ones results in a flat prior.


Stan code
We will now code this Poisson model in Stan.
data {
  int<lower=1> T; // Total number of months
  int<lower=1> T0; // End of pre-treatment period
  int<lower=1> K; // Number of donor countries
  array[T] int y; // Treated country migration counts (Ukraine)
  matrix[T, K] x; // Donor country migration counts/rates
}
parameters {
  real alpha;
  simplex[K] weights;
}
transformed parameters {
  vector[T] lambda;
  lambda = exp(alpha) * (x * weights);
}
model {
  // likelihood
  y[1 : T0] ~ poisson(lambda[1 : T0]);
  
  // priors
  alpha ~ normal(0, 10);
  weights ~ dirichlet(rep_vector(1, K));
}
generated quantities {
  array[T] int y_synthetic;
  array[T] int effect;
  
  for (t in 1 : T) {
    y_synthetic[t] = poisson_rng(lambda[t]);
    effect[t] = y[t] - y_synthetic[t];
  }
}
Notice that we are only including data in the likelihood for the pre-intervention period (i.e. [1:T0]). This is essential for the synthetic control model to represent pre-intervention expectations.
Note that we included a generated quantities block to produce posterior predictions across all time steps (i.e. y_synthetic[1:T]) which we will use as our synthetic control. These posterior predictions take into account the expectation from our scaled weighted average (\(\lambda_{k,t}\)) as well as the uncertainty (unexplained variance) associated with the Poisson distribution.
Save this Stan model code into a file named poisson.stan in the outdir that you defined above.

Important: If you don’t save the Stan model to this file, the code below will fail!



Select countries
In this example, we will look at migration out of Ukraine as a result of the large scale Russian invasion in February of 2022. Our goal is to build a synthetic estimate of migration without the war so that we can quantify the difference compared to observed migration. We can assess any destination country, but let’s start with Germany (DE).

destination <- 'DE' # Germany

# identify last month before the intervention

  pivot_wider(

# identify pre-treatment months

Lastly, we need to format the data for our model into a list object that is required by Stan.

# set seed for random number generators (important for reproducibility)
seed <- round(runif(1, 1, 1e6))
set.seed(seed)

# stan model data object
md <- list(
  T = length(months),
  T0 = which(row.names(x_donors) == last_pretreatment_month),
  K = length(donors),
  y = y_treated,
  x = x_donors_scaled,
  seed = seed
)

# save data to disk
saveRDS(
  object = md,
  file = file.path(outdir, "md.rds")
)



Markov chain Monte Carlo
Let’s actualy run MCMC to fit the model now!
It’s always good practice to create a function to generate random initial values for the MCMC chains.

# function to generate initials
init_generator <- function(md = md, chain_id = 1) {
  result <- list(
    alpha = rnorm(1, log(mean(md$y[1:md$T0])), 0.1),
    weights = rep(1 / md$K, md$K)
  )
  return(result)
}

# generate random initials for four chains
inits <- lapply(1:4, function(id) {
  init_generator(md = md, chain_id = id)
})

Now let’s compile and run the model:

# compile the stan model
mod <- cmdstan_model(file.path(outdir, "poisson.stan"))

# run MCMC
fit_po <- mod$sample(
  data = md, # model data (generated above)
  init = inits, # initials (generated above)
  parallel_chains = 4, # number of MCMC chains
  iter_warmup = 1e3, # warmup MCMC iterations to discard
  iter_sampling = 2e3, # MCMC iterations to keep
  seed = md$seed
)

# save model to disk
fit_po$save_object(file.path(outdir, "fit_poisson.rds"))



MCMC Diagnostics
Before looking at the substantive results, we need to do a quick sanity check just to confirm that the MCMC results are giving us reliable parameter estimates. Let’s take a look at a few traceplots to get a visual confirmation that chains are behaving well.


Show the R code
draws <- fit_po$draws()
pars <- c("alpha", paste0("weights[", sample(1:md$K, 11), "]"))

p <- mcmc_trace(draws, pars)
print(p)









These traceplots look great, but we need to check the r-hat statistic for each parameter to formally confirm that everything converged (i.e. rhat < 1.01). We can check this in the fit summary alongside our parameter estimates. Just sort this table by the rhat column to check for any unconverged parameters.


Show the R code
# get fit summary
fit_summary <- fit_po$summary()

# print summary to table

  column_to_rownames('variable') %>%
  round(4) %>%
  datatable(
    options = list(
      pageLength = 25,
      scrollX = TRUE,
      scrollY = "400px",
      fixedHeader = TRUE
    ),
    filter = 'top',
    rownames = TRUE
  )








Results
Now that we have confidence that the MCMC chains are converged, we’ll plot the synthetic control results.


Show the R code
# extract the posterior predictions for y_synthetic
draws_df <- fit_po$draws(
  variables = "y_synthetic",
  format = "df"
)

# summarise posterior predictions (mean, lower, upper)
synth_draws <- draws_df %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("y_synthetic"),
    names_to = "parameter",
    values_to = "value"
  ) %>%
  mutate(t = as.integer(gsub(".*\\[(\\d+)\\]", "\\1", parameter))) %>%
  group_by(t) %>%
  summarise(
    y_hat = mean(value),
    lower = quantile(value, 0.025),
    upper = quantile(value, 0.975),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(date = months[t])

# observed (real) data
real_data <- data.frame(
  date = row.names(md$x),
  y_obs = md$y
)

# data for plot
